query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high‐entropy alloys, an increased degree of short-range chemical ordering (SRO) amplifies the local heterogeneous lattice strain by creating zones of elevated shear-fault energy that more effectively pin dislocations. This combined effect increases hardness and yield strength relative to alloys with similar elemental compositions but with disrupted or minimal SRO.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, near‐equiatomic FCC high‐entropy alloy (e.g. NiCoCrFeMn) that inherently shows lattice distortion due to atomic size mismatch.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled thermal processing route: one set of samples is annealed at a moderate temperature to promote the formation of SRO, while a parallel set is rapidly quenched or subjected to severe plastic deformation to suppress SRO.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing (tensile and nanoindentation) conducted at room temperature and moderate strain rates with similar grain sizes in both sets; independent characterization of the degree of SRO must be performed via atom probe tomography or high-resolution diffraction to ensure the only significant difference is the SRO extent.
generation.structural_mediator: Local fluctuations in shear-fault (and related antiphase boundary) energies produced by chemically ordered clusters, which act in synergy with inherent heterogeneous lattice distortions to pin dislocations.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced SRO creates spatial variations in local energy barriers that force dislocations to navigate a rugged energy landscape. This ‘nanoscale detrapping’ process increases the resistance to dislocation motion compared to the baseline case, where lattice distortion alone governs pinning. The combined action results in higher macroscopic hardness and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with promoted SRO are predicted to exhibit significantly higher yield strength and nanoindentation hardness (on the order of a ~15–30% increase relative to the baseline random solid solution) due to intensified dislocation pinning, while samples with disrupted SRO will show mechanical properties closely matching predictions based solely on homogeneous lattice distortion.
generation.baseline: High‐entropy alloy samples processed such that SRO is minimal (via rapid quenching or heavy deformation), where the only strengthening mechanism is that from the heterogeneous lattice distortion inherent to the multi‐element mixture.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold in single-phase, near-equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloys at ambient temperature and moderate strain rates, where grain boundary and precipitate effects are minimal. It may not extend to multi-phase alloys, those with significant precipitation, or under extreme temperature/strain rate conditions where diffusion or other mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the findings of heterogeneous lattice strain-induced strengthening (PMC9231497) and the observed dislocation pinning and turbulent dislocation behavior induced by SRO (PMC10990144), by positing a direct causal link between degree of SRO and increased local energy barrier fluctuations. Uncertainty remains in quantifying SRO’s contribution independently from other mechanisms, and in accurately correlating measured SRO with the local shear-fault energy distribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples (same composition and grain size). Process one set by annealing at a moderate temperature to promote SRO formation, and process the other by rapid quenching or via heavy plastic deformation to suppress SRO. Verify the SRO level in each set using atom probe tomography or high-resolution diffraction before conducting mechanical tests.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of SRO extent in each set
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to image dislocation configurations and pinning sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-SRO samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength (or show similar dislocation pinning behavior) relative to the low-SRO baseline, then the hypothesis—that enhanced SRO in these alloys leads to improved hardness and strength—is falsified.

In particular, the local atomic distributions and their propensity for chemical ordering in HEAs have garnered much interest recently. Conceptually, our paper shows that systematic control of the nature and qualitative extent of ordering in HEAs is possible, starting from simple thermodynamic binary heats of mixing considerations and correlating that with corresponding mechanical properties. SignificanceImproving both the strength and ductility of metal materials has always been a great challenge for a long time. Our work shows the underlying physical characteristics of chemical short-range order in multi-principal element alloys, which causes higher strain peaks and wider strain wavelengths compared to traditional alloys. Remarkably, the heterogeneous lattice strain field induces a unique dislocation turbulent behavior and forms a special dislocation structure that is both a source and a trap at the vortex point, significantly enhancing both strength and ductility. SignificanceMulti–principal element alloys exhibit outstanding mechanical properties owing to severe atomic lattice distortion. However, the heterogeneous strain caused by lattice distortion at the microscopic or mesoscopic scale has been ignored for a long time because the heterogeneous strain field is difficult to quantify and characterize. Our experiments and simulations clearly show that the heterogeneous strain field can contribute to the enhanced mechanical properties of multi–principal element alloys through the new heterogeneous strain-induced strengthening mechanisms, leading to the strength-ductility synergy in severely distorted compositionally complex crystals. Multi–principal element alloys (MPEAs) exhibit outstanding mechanical properties because the core effect of severe atomic lattice distortion is distinctly different from that of traditional alloys. However, at the mesoscopic scale the underlying physics for the abundant dislocation activities responsible for strength-ductility synergy has not been uncovered.
